A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DSR framework and PRIME benchmark. Their text, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and relocated or renumbered material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original autoformalization experiments on ProverBench, ProofNet, and PRIME, including training and repair ablations and repair case studies.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds FATE evaluations, human validation of LeanScorer, decomposition accuracy measurements, and inference-time results.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same decomposition, joint code/OPT generation, curriculum training, assembly, and hierarchical repair procedures. The mandatory statement-level semantic check already appears in v1. Appendix B.5 explains existing safeguards, while the shortened decomposition prompt does not establish a substantive procedural change.

E1.justification: Appendix B.3 adds FATE-M, FATE-H, and FATE-X, extending evaluation to mathematical statements explicitly stressing intricate cross-statement and cross-line dependencies at multiple difficulty levels. The original three benchmarks and training corpus are retained.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds ATF-8B-Distilled and ATF-32B under both pass@4 and global repair. The original comparator set and DSR-Global remain; their repair comparisons were merged from v1 Table 4 rather than newly introduced. Appendix B.5 additionally compares the chosen Gemini decomposer with Qwen3-Max.

E3.justification: Beyond the retained SC/CC evaluation, v2 introduces human assessment of DSR and Goedel-V2-Formalizer-32B outputs across PRIME, comparing two evaluators with the same DeepSeek-V3.2 backbone using precision, recall, accuracy, and agreement metrics. It also adds manual decomposition evaluation on 90 randomly sampled statements, 30 per original benchmark. These substantially expand the evaluation design without changing the documented training settings.

E4.justification: New analyses examine PRIME overlap, evaluator agreement and disagreement with humans, decomposition accuracy, and inference-time costs (Appendices B.1, B.2, B.5, and B.6). The overlap analysis reports four conceptually similar FATE-M problems among PRIME's 156 entries. Existing training ablations, repair ablations, and repair cases are retained rather than replaced.

E5.justification: Table 4 newly reports statistical agreement with human judgments through Cohen's kappa: 0.766 for LeanScorer and 0.603 for direct LLM judging. This adds agreement estimation, but neither version reports confidence intervals, repeated-run variability, seed information, or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: All original main-result rows and both training-ablation tables retain their numerical values. Substantial new results cover ATF, evaluator validation, decomposition, timing, and FATE. On FATE-M/H/X, DSR reports CC rates of 77.33/41.00/11.00%, below Goedel-V2-Formalizer-32B's pass@4 results of 81.33/42.00/13.00%. Appendix B.5 reports decomposition accuracy of 95.56% for Gemini versus 87.78% for Qwen3-Max.

T1.justification: The OPT definition and mathematical reasoning underlying the framework are retained. Neither version provides formal theoretical guarantees or proofs; the added Lean examples illustrate dataset overlap rather than introduce theoretical results.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the modular DSR framework, the 156-theorem PRIME benchmark, and claimed state-of-the-art performance under matched budgets. v2 emphasizes novelty, benchmark reliability, and comparisons with larger models, but these reiterate the existing contribution scope rather than establish materially different core claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of contamination risk, LeanScorer's conservative errors, decomposition-error mitigation, FATE performance, and compiler-dominated runtime. Its impact statement adds automation-bias and computational-access concerns. Appendix A's limitations remain unchanged, but new assertions that leakage is eliminated and final semantic fidelity is guaranteed are stronger than the presented evidence establishes.

D1.justification: The abstract newly supplies a repository pointer announcing datasets, model, and code availability. Appendix B.6 discloses approximately 400 generated tokens, a 2048-token limit, sequential single-item repair execution, and measured inference times. These are focused additions to reproducibility information; the existing training hyperparameters remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Related work now explicitly distinguishes DRIFT's retrieval-oriented decomposition from DSR's structural decomposition and suggests combining them. FATE is newly cited, while ProofFlow is removed. ASSESS's updated publication details refer to the same previously cited work.

P1.justification: v2 makes targeted rewrites to contributions, results discussion, conclusion, and impact statement, and condenses the decomposition prompt. The appendices regroup retained ablations and case studies within an expanded Appendix B, with prompts moving from E to D. Most methodological prose and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v1 Tables 2 and 4 are consolidated into a substantially expanded Table 2. Four new tables display evaluator agreement, cross-model judgments, FATE results, and inference times; the existing end-to-end ablation becomes Table 7. Existing repair figures are reordered and renumbered, not newly added. These changes substantially reorganize the presentation of evidence.

improvement.justification: The human comparison addresses v1's reliance on LeanScorer without paper-specific human validation, while evaluator error analysis makes the semantic scores more interpretable. FATE testing exposes limits to DSR's dominance, and decomposition and timing analyses improve practical assessability. These substantially strengthen empirical credibility despite overconfident contamination and semantic-guarantee language, and headline claims that are not fully qualified by the second-best FATE consistency results.
